title: Merge Point
statement: Delivery routes are stored in one shared pool of stops. next[i] is the stop that follows stop i, or -1 when stop i is the last stop of its route. Route A begins at stop headA and route B begins at stop headB. Because every stop has exactly one follower, two routes that share a stop also share every stop after it. Return the index of the first stop on route A that also lies on route B, or -1 if the routes never share a stop. Do not change next.
constraints: Every next[i] is -1 or a valid stop index, and following next from any stop always reaches -1 (no route loops back)

examples.explanation: Route A is 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 and route B is 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Stop 4 is the first stop of A that also lies on B.
Route A is 0, 1 and route B is 2, 3. They never share a stop.

hints.content: Once two routes reach the same stop they stay together to the end, because every stop has only one follower.
For each stop on route A you could walk all of route B looking for it. How many steps is that in the worst case?
If you remember route A's stops in a set, a single walk down route B finds the first match. That is fast but needs memory proportional to route A.
Let each pointer walk its own route and then continue from the head of the other route. After that, both pointers have covered the same total number of stops.
Move both pointers one stop at a time with that switching rule until they point at the same stop. If the routes never join, both reach -1 on the same step, and the loop ends returning -1.

testCases.explanation: Both routes start at the same stop, so it is the answer.
Route B passes through A's first stop, so the answer is A's head.
A is 0, 1, 2, 5 and B is 3, 4, 2, 5; the first shared stop on A is 2.
Large pool: two routes of 6000 stops each, with lead-ins of equal length (4000 stops each) ending in a shared 2000-stop tail, so both pointers reach the join on the same step without a swap.
Large pool where the two routes have very different lengths before they join.
Large pool with two separate long routes: the answer is -1.

solutions.title: Compare every pair of stops
solutions.intuition: The answer is the first stop of A that equals some stop of B, so test every pair.
solutions.approach: Walk route A. For each stop, walk all of route B and return the stop as soon as the two walks hit the same index.
solutions.pseudocode:
for a on route A: for b on route B: if a == b: return a
return -1
commonMistakes: Comparing the values stored in the stops instead of their indexes.
Skipping the heads: headA itself may lie on route B (even equal headB), so the first stop of A must be compared too.
solutions.interviewExplanation: This nested walk is the direct reading of the statement. It uses no extra memory but costs lenA times lenB steps, which is too slow for long routes.

steps.title: Try stop 0 of route A
steps.content: In the first example, 0 is compared with 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and never matches.

steps.title: Reach the join
steps.content: Stop 1 does not match either. Stop 4 matches B's third stop, so 4 is returned.

solutions.title: Remember route A in a set
solutions.intuition: Replace the inner walk with a constant-time membership test.
solutions.approach: Add every stop of route A to a set. Then walk route B and return the first stop that is in the set. Because B's walk reaches shared stops in route order, and the shared part is a common tail, the first hit is the first shared stop.
solutions.pseudocode:
seen = set(route A)
for stop on route B: if stop in seen: return stop
return -1
commonMistakes: Adding only the stops reached through next to the set and not the head of route A, which misses a head that also lies on route B.
solutions.interviewExplanation: A hash set turns the quadratic search into two linear walks. It costs memory proportional to one route, which the pointer-switching version avoids.

steps.title: Walk route B
steps.content: Stops 2 and 3 are not in the set; stop 4 is, so the answer is 4.

solutions.title: Walk both routes, then swap
solutions.intuition: If each pointer walks its own route and then the other one, both cover lenA + lenB stops, so they line up on the join stop.
solutions.approach: Start a at headA and b at headB. Step both forward. When one reaches -1, move it to the head of the other route. Stop when a === b: that stop is the merge point, or -1 when neither route joins the other.
solutions.pseudocode:
a = headA; b = headB
while a != b:
  a = (a == -1) ? headB : next[a]
  b = (b == -1) ? headA : next[b]
return a
commonMistakes: Switching when the pointer is on the last real stop instead of after it reaches -1, which skips the case where the routes end at the same last stop.
Not letting -1 act as a stop, which loops forever when the routes never join.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Let a = stops only on A, b = stops only on B and c = shared stops. Pointer one travels a + c, then switches and travels b before reaching the shared part; pointer two travels b + c and then a. Both have then walked a + b stops and stand on the first shared stop together. If c = 0, both reach -1 after a + b + 1 steps in total and are equal there. It runs in O(lenA + lenB) time and O(1) extra space.

steps.title: Start both pointers
steps.content: In the first example a walks 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 and b walks 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

steps.title: Swap on reaching -1
steps.content: a moves on to stop 2, b moves on to stop 0 after their routes end.

steps.title: They meet
steps.content: After lenA + lenB steps the pointers both stand on stop 4. When the routes never join they both land on -1.
